introFa: کتاب «Political Order and Political Decay: From the Industrial Revolution to the Globalization of Democracy» نوشته Francis Fukuyama یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Political Order and Political Decay: From the Industrial Revolution to the Globalization of Democracy»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Critical Dialogue Political Order and Political Decay: From the Industrial Revolution to the Globalization of Democracy. By Francis Fukuyama. New York: Farrar, Strauss and Giroux, 2014. 672p. $35.00 cloth, $18.00 paper. doi:10.1017/S1537592717000500 — Carles Boix, Princeton University Back in the 1960s, as the social sciences matured into the methodological and theoretical forms we practice today, two books shaped the study of comparative politics in a decisive way: Barrington Moore’s Social Origins of Democracy and Dictatorship (1966) and Samuel Hunting- ton’s Political Order in Changing Societies (1968). In his new book, Francis Fukuyama takes on and extends the research agenda of both scholars—with a main focus, however, on Huntington’s research agenda. Fukuyama’s choice makes sense. In the last decades, the study of political regimes and political transitions has been culti- vated intensively, reaching, in Fukuyama’s own words, a theoretical framework that, rooted in Moore’s work, is “with a few emendations . . . basically sound” (p. 411). By contrast, the examination of political order and decay has been sparser. Putting aside the literature on state formation spurred by Charles Tilly and Mancur Olson and a growing body of work on civil wars, we still know little about the determinants of state capacity and quality of government. In Huntington’s book, political stability depended on the presence of “strong, adaptable, coherent political institutions” capable of channeling the processes of social mobilization unleashed by economic modernization. The Anglo-American world succeeded in retaining its tradi- tional Tudor institutions and adapting them organically to modern society. The developing world had the almost exact reverse experience. The state was too weak to cope with the popular demands brought about by development. Structural conditions, such as the gap between city and countryside or land inequality, mattered in order to achieve stability. But for Huntington—a “Leninist” where Moore had been a “Marxist”—order was ultimately created by a revolutionary (or a reformist) vanguard through a political party (or parties) that could stabilize mass politics. Fukuyama follows in Huntington’s footsteps in his preoccupation with political stability and institutions. However, Political Order and Political Decay unpacks the concept of political order into three dimensions—a stable and capable state, the rule of law, and (democratic) accountability—claiming that they are independent of one another: In some nations (like Denmark), they are bundled together; in others (like Somalia), they are all absent; and in many countries, only some are in place (like China, with a capable state but no rule of law). Hence, following “Huntington’s basic instinct,” political modern- ization has not been “a seamless and inevitable process” (p. 50) but has, rather, followed multiple, sometimes inchoate and broken, developmental paths. Premodern societies were Malthusian economies gov- erned by patrimonial states, “staffed with the friends and family of the ruler,” who “limited access to both political power and economic opportunity to individuals [he] favored” (p. 198), and they sustained power through patron–client networks. Political modernization took place along three alternative historical paths, each deﬁned by the speciﬁc temporal sequence through which state, the rule of law, and accountability emerged. In the Anglo- American world, the rule of law preceded economic growth; mass democracy followed next (before the in- dustrial revolution in the United States and during industrialization in England); and a strong state (understood as a Weberian bureaucracy employing merit-based recruitment criteria) came in last. In the German path (shared by Japan and other East Asian tigers), countries moved into modernity through the creation of a modern bureaucracy ﬁrst and the adoption of the rule of law and democracy much later (brought in, to a considerable extent, by military defeat and foreign intervention). China developed along that same route, albeit in an incomplete way: Democracy and the rule of law are still missing. Finally, the third historical path, which characterizes, with various degrees of intensity, parts of Southeastern Europe, Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa, is one of “modernization without development.” The emergence of “mass politics” (and democracy), with neither a strong Weberian state nor the rule of law in place, resulted in two possible scenarios: either political decay or “a stable system of clientelism and elite coalitions built around the distribution of rents” (p. 530). Absent a process of industrialization and a corresponding modern middle class that could carry out the modernization policies that the American middle classes implemented © American Political Science Association 2017 June 2017 | Vol. 15/No. 2 567 Critical Dialogues https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592717000512

in the nineteenth century to weed out the clientelistic networks of Jacksonian democracy, those countries have no prospects of “getting to Denmark,” that is, “an imagined society that is prosperous, democratic, secure, and well governed” (p. 25). Fukuyama’s basic intuition about the need to disaggre- gate political development into several dimensions is correct. It is unfortunate, however, that the book does not deal with the expansion and consolidation of the rule of law in the same systematic way it does for state capacity. As for the latter, it has at least two meanings: the capacity to maintain the monopoly of force over a given population and territory, and state capacity as quality of performance. The former is treated by Fukuyama in The Origins of Political Order (2011), preceding the book reviewed here. Political Order and Political Decay focuses on the latter: Its examination is impressive and thought provoking. After pointing out that there is no “scholarly agreement on a standardized way of measuring state quality” (p. 61), Fukuyama ﬁrst embraces a well-known outcome measure, the World Bank’s government effectiveness index, to capture state capacity (as quality of performance). But right afterward he identiﬁes it with the introduction of a rational or Weberian bureaucracy, that is, an autono- mous public administration run by personnel selected on merit principles and deciding according to technical principles (either legal rationality or scientiﬁc manage- ment). Indeed, having a modern bureaucracy is likely to be a necessary condition to having a capable state. But the book would have beneﬁted from deploying more direct evidence showing that a merit-based bureaucracy leads to (or is correlated with) government effectiveness. Perhaps more importantly, the book does not clarify whether a Weberian state is a sufﬁcient condition for having good institutional performance. Just consider today’s Chinese state. Its “Weberianism” seems very limited, with elites having a strong say in the discriminatory allocation of rents to allies. Yet it arguably is a strong state, capable of coercing people and mobilizing resources quite effectively. In a way, that seems to vindicate Huntington’s theory: It may well be that the Chinese state is strong because the Chinese Communist Party (rather than China’s bureau- cracy) vertebrates it. Finally, Fukuyama does not spell out whether having a Weberian bureaucracy is endogenous to other historical conditions. According to Robert Putnam, for example, even though Italy’s regional institutions were identical, their performance depended on their level of social capital and civic engagement and how they affected, in turn, personnel recruitment and the allocation of resources. The theory that the three dimensions of political development are independent of one another also calls for more debate. On the one hand, a weak state seems incompatible with having the rule of law (deﬁned in the book as “rules of behavior . . . binding even the most powerful political actors in the society” (p. 24)), since a patrimonial state implies the unequal access of individ- uals to state positions and resources. On the other hand, strong states with Weberian bureaucracies may not always come together with the rule of law. But even that eventuality needs to be qualiﬁed: A Weberian bureaucracy is always founded on the application of universal principles (or the rule of law) in the particular sphere (administrative decision making) where it operates; without them, it collapses into a clientelistic structure. A similar problem arises with the relationship between rule of law and accountability. Without a full franchise making all indi- viduals equal, the “binding” condition that deﬁnes the rule of law cannot be fulﬁlled. The latter remains limited to the sphere of private law while excluding the domain of political rights—the case of imperial Germany or Victorian England. The book’s description of several political moderniza- tion trajectories is a stepping stone in our understanding of contemporary state building. Still, future researchers will have to deal with at least two questions left open by the author. First, by overemphasizing the distinctiveness of the East Asian, Latin American and sub-Saharan African historical paths, this volume underplays a high degree of variation within each continent. Countries such as Botswana, South Africa, Chile, or Mexico show similar or higher scores than China in the World Bank govern- ment effectiveness index. This must mean that twentieth- century developments (examined in the book through Argentina, Costa Rica, and Indonesia, but not systemat- ically) eventually overcame “longue-durée” constraints that had been operating at the continental level. Second, the relationship between political and economic develop- ment remains unclear. As in Huntington, and in opposi- tion to Moore’s insistence on the primacy of social interests, Fukuyama writes that political development “follows its own logic independent of economic growth” (p. 50) and that, contrary to the claims of economic institutionalists, growth happened both in places with the rule of law and a weak state (England) and with no rule of law but a strong state (Japan, China). Still, at some other points, the book makes political modernization endoge- nous to economic development—particularly when we are told that countries without a strong state have “no clear path from informal employment to true growth- and job- generating industrialization” (p. 531), something that, in turn, prevented them from reforming. While in the last decades we have made some headway in measuring and theorizing about phenomena such as political stability, democratization, or civil wars, progress in understanding the nature and sources of state capacity and performance has proved to be much more elusive to us. For that reason, Political Order and Political Decay is an important contribution to the study of politics: it brings in both a conceptually savvy discussion and a fascinating 568 Perspectives on Politics Critical Dialogues https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592717000512

historical exploration of the development of states since the French Revolution. At the same time, and perhaps because of its scope, it will certainly require and stimulate more work on the relationship between bureaucratic structures and state capacity, between the latter and the rule of law, and between economic and political development. Response to Carles Boix’s review of Political Order and Political Decay: From the Industrial Revolution to the Globalization of Democracy doi:10.1017/S1537592717000512 — Francis Fukuyama I very much appreciate Carles Boix’s review of Political Order and Political Decay, and would in fact agree with him about many of the things that are missing from my book. Let me respond to several of the speciﬁc points he raises. A central issue concerns Boix’s observation that my three institutional legs—state, rule of law, and accountability—are not entirely independent of one another. State and rule of law in particular overlap considerably: The ability to enforce laws is both a compo- nent of state capacity and part of the rule of law. Rule of law and democracy, for their part, are alternative ways of constraining state power and often have worked hand in glove to that end. Nonetheless, separating these three pillars conceptually is critical. Many recent institutionalists (see Douglass C. North, John Wallis, and Barry R. Weingast, Violence and Social Orders: A Conceptual Frame- work for Interpreting Recorded Human History, 2009, and Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty, 2013) have not been sufﬁciently precise in distinguishing between them. As a result, they are not able to address long- standing questions, such as whether it is better to sequence introduction of a liberal rule of law prior to extending the franchise, or how the trade-off between state power and legal checks is to be made. Boix notes that I do not provide adequate evidence linking a state’s Weberian qualities to government per- formance and, later on, to economic growth. This is, in fact, one of the most understudied issues in contemporary political science. One such effort was that of Peter Evans and James Rauch (“Bureaucratic Structure and Bureau- cratic Performance in Less Developed Countries,” Journal of Public Economics 75 [2000]: 49–71), who did in fact see this linkage, but they covered only 37 countries and it was never followed up in a systematic way. More recently, Bo Rothstein (The Quality of Government: Corruption, Social Trust, and Inequality in International Perspective, 2011) has done a number of studies that show a good correlation between impartiality, which is arguably at the core of a Weberian state, and a variety of measures of state performance. Others like Katherine Bersch, Sérgio Praça, and Matthew M. Taylor (“State Capacity, Bureaucratic Politicization, and Corruption in the Brazilian State,” Governance, n.d.) have linked the Weberian characteristics of autonomy and capacity to performance in a single country (Brazil), but do not extend this cross-nationally. This is an area where much more research needs to be done. Finally, Boix is correct to point out that my book— unlike his—does not establish a clear link between the different institutional characteristics I emphasize and eco- nomic growth. That is correct; my primary aim was to explain political rather than economic development. My general observation is that there are probably some minimal institutions necessary for growth. But contrary to many contemporary institutionalists, there is not a clear set of institutional conditions that are either necessary or sufﬁcient to explain historically observed growth (see Ricardo Haus- mann, Lant Pritchett, and Dani Rodrik, “Growth Accel- erations.” Journal of Economic Growth, 10 [no. 4, 2005]: 303–29). This is the problem with macro theorizing about development more generally: The underlying phenomenon is so complex that most elegant theories reducing explan- atory variables to a small number are likely to fail. Nonethe- less, we have to keep trying, and I appreciate Carles Boix’s important contributions to this effort. Political Order and Inequality: Their Foundations and Their Consequences for Human Welfare. By Carles Boix. New York: Cambridge University Press, 2015. 334p. $67.00 cloth, $23.99 paper. doi:10.1017/S1537592717000524 — Francis Fukuyama, Stanford University Carles Boix has written a very impressive book, full of novel sources of data and insights about the intertwined processes of economic and political development. In it he draws heavily on prior work like his 2003 Democracy and Redistribution, but combines those arguments with highly innovative approaches to the empirical study of early societies that existed prior to the advent of writing and historical records. While much of the development ﬁeld has focused on randomized experiments that necessarily consider micro issues, Boix is unafraid to take on the largest of macro questions. He is writing very much in the tradition of two other recent efforts to present a uniﬁed theory of development that encompasses the phenomenon’s eco- nomic and political dimensions: Violence and Social Orders: A Conceptual Framework for Interpreting Recorded Human History (Douglass North, John Wallis, and Barry Weingast, 2009) and Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty (Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, 2012). June 2017 | Vol. 15/No. 2 569 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592717000512

Political Order and Inequality both builds on and goes considerably beyond these neoinstitutionalist writers. Boix argues that North, Wallis, and Weingast overemphasize parliaments, formal property rights, and constitutional settlements like the Glorious Revolution of 1689 in their account of the rise of modern “open access” orders. They neglect military competition and the way that evolving military technologies favor speciﬁc social groups; thus, the use of the horse and the iron stirrup increased inequality by giving military advantages to the aristocracy. Boix points out that there were actually two equilibria that emerged in the early modern period, the monarchical one emphasized by North, Wallis, and Weingast and a republican one that existed in Italy, the Netherlands, and of course North America, where power was held by a broader oligarchy. Which form ended up prevailing depended on the balance of power between “looters” (i.e., the predatory armed aristocracy) and “producers” (i.e., merchants and early capitalists, p. 65) as they made use of military technologies from the gun to the trace italienne. While military dominance is related to general economic growth, it is not coterminous with it; hence, mounted predators from Central Asia could dominate richer agrarian societies for many centuries. With regard to Acemoglu and Robinson, Boix notes quite properly that their deﬁnition of good institutions is so broad that “instead of explaining (the absence of) growth, it turns the outcome that we can explain . . . into the explanation itself” (p. 221). One of the great virtues of Political Order and Inequality is its creative use of new data sets to illuminate several important historical transitions. Thus, for example, in explaining the rise of states out of “foraging societies,” Boix makes use of the Ethnographic Atlas that covers more than 1,100 early societies, and is able to correlate political outcomes like state formation and social hierarchy against a wide variety of biogeographical variables, such as population density, domesticatible animal species, and exogenous technological shocks. Similarly, he uses data on height distributions in primitive societies as a proxy for income inequality in societies for which no recorded income data is available, making use of Franz Boas’s famous data set gathered from living Native Americans early in the twentieth century. Boix shows that in primitive societies, inequality increased with the introduction of agriculture and the growth of early states, and decreased with the spread of republican governments in the modern era, as well as being affected by the introduction of certain military technologies like the horse. This analysis mostly conﬁrms what anthropologists have believed for some time, placing these ﬁndings on a much broader empirical foundation. The book thus usefully critiques and extends existing rational choice models of political development, adding as a separate independent variable the evolution of military technologies, and demonstrating the possibility of alter- native equilibrium outcomes—particularly the republican one—as a result. Unlike either the North-Wallis-Weingast or Acemoglu-Robinson volumes, which do not explain change over time, Boix presents a developmental theory in which endogenous change in both production and military technologies drives the major political and economic transitions in human history. The limitations of this approach are related to its rational choice framework more broadly, that is, a frame- work that assumes that human behavior can be explained as the result of interactions of selﬁsh but rational individuals seeking to maximize their utilities. Boix’s ﬁrst chapter, entitled “Tabula Rasa,” begins deductively from the assumption that early human beings lived in a state of anarchy, and began to spontaneously organize their interactions through rational calculation of self-interest. This assumption is contradicted by much of what is now known about evolutionary psychology and early primate and human behavior. As noted by Melvin Konner (The Tangled Wing: Biological Constraints on the Human Spirit, 1982), Carl Degler (In Search of Human Nature: The Decline and Revival of Darwinism in American Social Thought, 1991), and Steven Pinker (The Blank Slate; The Modern Denial of Human Nature, 2002), the human mind was never the blank slate imagined by John Locke or contemporary neoclassical economists. Rather, it is ﬁlled with evolved structures that promote social cooperation, not as a matter of rational choice but through faculties rooted in the emotions. Kin selection and reciprocal altruism are hard-wired into primate brains; early human groups as well as the higher primates from which they evolved never lived in a state of anarchy. It is true that rates of violence have decreased over the 50,000 or so years that behaviorally modern human beings have existed (Norbert Elias, ed. [1978], The Civilizing Process: The History of Manners; Lawrence Keeley [1996], War Before Civiliza- tion; Steven Pinker [2011], The Better Angels of Our Nature: Why Violence Has Declined; and Ian Morris [2014], War: What Is It Good For?). However, this has been the product of successive forms of social organization that simply increased the scale on which societies could be paciﬁed. By lumping all prestate-level forms of social organiza- tion into a single “forager” category, Boix misses one of the most important transitions in early human social organization, the shift from band-level societies to tribal ones, or, in anthropological terms, to societies based on segmentary lineages. In the latter type of society, individ- uals trace their descent to a common ancestor who could be several generations removed; this allowed the vast scaling up in the size of social organizations and is the reason why lineage-based or tribal societies could over- whelm band-level groups that usually consisted of no more than 50 to 100 closely related individuals. 570 Perspectives on Politics Critical Dialogues https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592717000512

The development model presented in Political Order and Inequality is relentlessly materialistic: Boix asserts that “self-interest dominates the external or social behavior of individuals in stateless societies” (p. 249) and dismisses Weber’s theories about the role of religion in the transition to modernity (pp. 206, 255). The words “religion” and “legitimacy” do not appear anywhere in the book’s index. Yet while speciﬁc theories like those of Weber may be contested, ideas are critical to understanding all political transitions. For example, the shift from band- to tribal-level societies, which occurred in virtually every human society around 10,000 years ago, was based on a religious idea, that is, the power of dead ancestors and unborn descendants to affect one’s happiness in the present. Absent this ideational framework, it is not obvious why one should prefer cooperating with a third or fourth cousin one has never met over a friendly stranger. Indeed, loyalty to kin, based partly on human biology and partly on deeply embedded norms of ﬁctive kinship, meant that human societies stuck with lineage organizations long after they ceased to be functional. The transition to state-level societies, therefore, required extraordinary institutional arrangements in order to overcome this inertia, such as the Arab-Ottoman practice of capturing young non- Muslim boys and raising them to be soldiers and admin- istrators precisely because the indigenous population could not be shaken of tribal loyalties. This is a problem that continues to inhibit legitimate state formation in the contemporary Middle East. Similarly, the transition to modern liberal democracy cannot be explained without reference to ideas, in particular the idea of the universality of human dignity (Tocqueville [1835] 2000, Democracy in America). The material self-interest of different social classes—the old landowning oligarchy, the bourgeoisie, and rising proletariat—were of course critical social determinants of the spread of democracy. Boix’s earlier theory of the importance of mobile versus ﬁxed capital (Democracy and Redistribution) is a relevant part of this story. But the perceived self-interest of a social class is not simply determined by its economic position or by technology. In nineteenth-century Europe, proletarian class conscious- ness was undermined by an alternative form of mobiliza- tion based on the idea of nation, leading to two devastating world wars. As a result of this disaster, the way was paved for a fuller normative commitment to democracy in Europe after 1945. As Ernest Gellner (Nations and Nationalism, 2006) suggested, religion today plays a similar role in the Middle East, where Islam has displaced class self-interest as the dominant form of social mobilization. Political Order and Inequality commendably bucks the trend toward the ever more micro study of development, and brings new data to bear on many of the classical problems of social theory. It would be better, however, if the author saw the rational choice framework as a starting point for theory, rather than as a self-contained system capable of explaining the whole of human development. Response to Francis Fukuyama’s review of Political Order and Inequality: Their Foundations and Their Consequences for Human Welfare doi:10.1017/S1537592717000536 — Carles Boix In his generous review of Political Order and Inequality, Francis Fukuyama writes that the book’s limitations come from its commitment to a rational choice framework that models human beings as self-interest individuals and that forgets the independent role of ideas. Fukuyama afﬁrms, instead, that the human mind, “never the blank slate imagined by John Locke or contemporary neoclassical economists,” is both “ﬁlled with evolved structures that promote social cooperation . . . through faculties rooted in the emotions” and “hard-wired” for “kin selection and reciprocal altruism.” As a matter of fact, the book acknowledges that we have always lived in families and bands and that “affective or emotional reasons, such as the ties that bind parents and children together” (p. 32) play an important role in human cooperation. It recognizes, too, the role of reciprocal altruism, particularly in informal social interactions. In- deed, altruism as well as other moral senses (such as fairness or duty) seem to be universal dispositions in humans (cf. J. Q. Wilson’s The Moral Sense [2003]). The problem, however, is that this universality in moral predispositions clashes with the fact that actual social cooperation is rather limited and fragile (particularly without formal institutions). My answer is that even if we may be inclined to cooperate, the extent to which we do is fundamentally shaped by the economic and political structures explored in Political Order and Inequality. An alternative way to explain varying levels of human cooperation consists in asserting, ﬁrst, that the extent of altruistic sentiments varies across human communities (Jonathan Haidt and Selin Kesebir, “Morality,” in Susan T. Fiske et al., Handbook of Social Psychology, 2010) and, second, that less developed societies have or had a weaker predisposition to altruism than modern ones (cf. Edward Banﬁeld’s work on amoral familism and more recent work by economist Ernst Fehr and coauthors). In that alternative account, some critical historical moments or shocks would have arguably ampliﬁed the altruistic orientation of humans. Those shocks would have been of two kinds: material shocks (e.g., the agrarian revolu- tion) that would have reshaped the predisposition to cooperate for the optimization reasons defended by functionalism and that I criticize in my book; and ideational shocks of the kind examined by Max Weber June 2017 | Vol. 15/No. 2 571 https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592717000512

in his analysis of the economic consequences of Refor- mation and called for by Fukuyama. Mankind has indeed experienced important ideational shifts. In the domain of religious ideas, for example, there have been momentous changes both in the object of worship (evolving from animism through polytheism to Karl Jaspers’s axial religions) and in the relationship between spiritual and temporal powers. But to claim that religious (or any other kind of) ideas matter, we need to establish two things: that they are exogenous and that they have a causal impact on our outcome of interest. Looking here (for space limitations) at two cases (religion in the transition from bands to tribes or lineages, and the emergence of axial religions) should make us skeptical about the causal role of ideas (as worldviews or principled beliefs). Both bands and tribes worshipped ancestors and did not differ systematically in their beliefs about the existence of gods. Still, lineages probably worshipped a single ancestor (common to the lineage) while bands believed in many. Yet the exogeneity and the causality conditions are not met: The difference correlates with other fundamental material changes; it is unclear how the biogeographical parameters triggering those changes could lead to the religious shift directly; and such a minor religious transformation cannot account for their differences in social stratiﬁcation. In turn, the creation of axial religions (between 700 and 300 B.C.) seems exogenous to nonideational factors, but it cannot be matched to any subsequent key political or economic transformation. 572 Perspectives on Politics Critical Dialogues https://www.cambridge.org/core/terms. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1537592717000512
